hypothesis: Symbolic lexical/statistical engine with exact resolvers (pre-neural champion)
architecture: symbolic: BM25 + tf-idf + char n-grams + WordNet graph + negation scopes + 6 resolvers + conditional-logit fusion + temperature/Platt calibration
dataset_version: synthetic v2 + 12 permissive public datasets (24k records)
reason: pre-neural baseline measured on the frozen internal benchmark (3000 dev records)

hypothesis: H3 (diagnostic): is long-context failure caused by retrieval or by reasoning?
architecture: retrieval-only ablation of the symbolic evidence selector (BM25 pooled vs per-candidate quota vs adaptive budget)
dataset_version: data/bench_internal/long_context.jsonl (1548 questions with gold evidence annotations)

dev_metrics.measurement: evidence retrieval recall on data/bench_internal/long_context.jsonl (1548 questions with annotated gold evidence)
dev_metrics.metric: share of questions whose gold evidence sentences survive into the evidence block handed to the encoder
dev_metrics.conclusion: Lexical retrieval, not the decision head, is the dominant long-context failure: above 1k tokens the decisive sentence survives in under 10% of cases at a 140-word budget. Recall scales with the budget (0.28 -> 0.44 -> 0.57 at 140/300/600 words) but not to a usable level, so a learned retriever (or hierarchical chunk scoring) is required. Per-candidate quotas do not help at a small budget because the reserved slots are spent on decoy paragraphs that name the wrong options.

reason: per-candidate quotas at a 140-word budget are worse than pooled (0.145 vs 0.283 full recall); wider budgets help sub-linearly (0.28/0.44/0.57 at 140/300/600 words). Kept: document-order fallback and the adaptive budget (0.342 at cap 400). Conclusion recorded as the motivation for a learned retriever.

hypothesis: Pipeline validation: does the champion/challenger path (export -> probe -> fusion fit -> engine eval -> dev score) work end to end?
reason: toy model, as expected below the champion (dev_score 0.585 -> 0.488). Kept as the validation that the promotion pipeline runs and that the fusion fitter automatically down-weights a weak neural scorer (it chose weight_neural=0.5, weight_symbolic=1.0).

hypothesis: H16: the evidence retriever scores BM25 without a state-local document-frequency factor, so in long states common terms swamp the ranking; adding local idf (and expanding the question query with the criteria synonym sets) should raise evidence recall where it is worst
architecture: retrieval-only change to crates/core/src/export.rs: local_idf + q_expand switches on EvidenceParams, recorded per model in scorer.json
dataset_version: data/bench_internal/long_context.jsonl (1512 records, 1548 questions), internal synthetic, no JevBench
reason: Both switches improve evidence recall monotonically with no regression in any length bucket; gains concentrate in the long buckets (1k +4.2pts, 4k +3.9pts, 16k +4.0pts) exactly as the hypothesis predicted. A third idea tested in the same pass, boosting segments containing a candidate phrase near-verbatim, moved recall by 0.000 in every bucket and was removed from the tree. Adopted for training exports from E2 onward; E1 was already training against the old retriever and keeps local_idf=false in its scorer.json, so its parity is unaffected.

hypothesis: H13/H19: a learned linear ranker over the features retrieval already computes beats the pooled BM25 ordering
architecture: 16-feature linear ranker, listwise softmax over a state's segments, selected on budget recall at 140 words
dataset_version: data/retrieval/all.jsonl: 54553 lists from data/synthetic/bench_train.jsonl + bench_train_lc.jsonl, negatives capped at 60 per list, split 90/10 by record id
reason: Measurement invalid, no conclusion drawn about the hypothesis. Budget recall on the held-out slice was 0.9946 for the ranker and 0.9929 for the pooled-BM25 baseline: the metric is saturated because most training-pool records are under 128 tokens, so their entire state fits the 140-word budget and retrieval never has to choose. Capping negatives at 60 compounded it by shortening every list well below the hundreds of segments a real long state has. The fitted weights are therefore not trustworthy and are not being adopted. Re-running with the export restricted to questions whose state exceeds the budget and with every negative kept.

hypothesis: H13/H19: a learned linear ranker over the features retrieval already computes beats the pooled BM25 ordering on long states
architecture: 16-feature linear ranker (z-scores and rank percentiles of the question / pooled / best-candidate BM25 vectors, term coverage, char-4-gram containment, length ratio, document position, focus-field, number, date and negation flags, log segment count), listwise softmax over a state's segments, greedy budget fill by score
dataset_version: 8610 lists from data/synthetic/bench_train.jsonl + bench_train_lc.jsonl, restricted to states exceeding the 140-word budget, every negative kept, split 85/15 by record id
reason: Wins on the metric it was fitted to and loses on the one that matters. Budget recall on the held-out slice rose from 0.592 to 0.731 and top-1 from 0.601 to 0.712, but on the frozen long-context suite full evidence recall FELL from 0.306 to 0.238 and total losses rose from 0.504 to 0.625. Every length bucket at 256 tokens and above got worse, by 0.13 at 256, 0.22 at 512 and 0.12 at 16384; only the two buckets short enough to mostly bypass retrieval improved. By evidence position the loss is concentrated at the start (0.644 to 0.452) and split (0.605 to 0.499). Two causes, both plausible and both actionable. First, a metric mismatch: the fit optimises the fraction of annotated SEGMENTS retrieved, while the suite measures token-level containment of the gold STRINGS, so a ranker can retrieve the right number of segments and the wrong ones. Second, a template-pool shift: bench and train templates are disjoint by construction, and a weight of +4.03 on a binary negation flag is exactly the kind of generator artefact that will not survive that boundary. No retrieval.json is shipped, so production behaviour is unchanged and the heuristic ordering stands. The infrastructure is kept because it is the vehicle for the follow-ups, not because the ranker is adopted.

hypothesis: H24 + H25: fitting the ranker against the share of the annotated span each segment carries, and selecting it across a template boundary rather than a record boundary, fixes what sank R3
architecture: same 16-feature linear ranker as R3; listwise cross-entropy against the token-share target distribution instead of the log mass on binary positives; selection split on the record's structural template signature
dataset_version: 8610 lists from data/synthetic/bench_train.jsonl + bench_train_lc.jsonl, states exceeding the 140-word budget only, every negative kept; 7901 fitting / 709 selection over 518 / 126 structural signatures with none shared
reason: Both corrections worked and the ranker still does not beat the heuristic. On the template-held-out selection set budget recall rose from 0.548 to 0.750 and top-1 from 0.453 to 0.580. On the frozen long-context suite full evidence recall is 0.285 against the heuristic's 0.306: a real improvement on R3's 0.238, closing two thirds of that gap, but still short. The shape of the remaining gap is informative and specific. The ranker now WINS on short and medium states, 128 tokens +0.081 and 256 tokens +0.053, and on evidence placed at the end, +0.049. It loses on long states, 512 tokens -0.086 rising to -0.081 at 16k, and above all on evidence placed at the start, -0.136. That single position accounts for most of the deficit and points at the heuristic's document-order fallback, which spends leftover budget from segment zero and so bets that evidence sits early. A quarter of the suite places it exactly there. Whether the heuristic is a better ranker or merely holds a benchmark-shaped bet is now a measurable question, and the next run answers it by disabling the fallback. No artifact shipped.

hypothesis: H27: part of the heuristic's advantage at evidence-at-start is its document-order fallback rather than its ranking
architecture: ablation: heuristic evidence selection with the document-order fill disabled (--no-doc-order-fallback)
reason: The ablation does not test what it was meant to test, and saying so is the result. Disabling the fallback drops full recall from 0.306 to 0.160, but it also leaves the budget unspent: 526 of 1548 rows fall under 100 words of the 140 available, mean 104 against 135. Without the fallback the selector can only use segments BM25 scored above zero, and BM25 scores too few. So the fallback's contribution is mostly that it spends the budget at all, not that it bets on evidence being early, and the two cannot be separated this way. The comparison that matters is unaffected: the heuristic and the R4 ranker both spend essentially the whole budget, so heuristic 0.306 against ranker 0.285 is like for like. What the ablation does suggest is the next hypothesis. The fallback's fill is contiguous by construction, and the recall metric scores the longest unbroken run of gold tokens, so a span split across segments counts only as its largest fragment. An annotated span is a median 38 words and routinely runs across several segments, which a ranker picking the individually best segments will scatter. Recorded as H28 and tested next by gluing neighbours onto each ranked pick.

hypothesis: H28: retrieve contiguous neighbourhoods rather than independent segments, because an annotated span runs across several segments and taking the individually best ones returns it in pieces
architecture: retrieval-only: after each segment is chosen, also take N segments either side while the budget allows (EvidenceParams.neighbour_glue). Applies to both the heuristic ordering and the learned-ranker path.
reason: The largest retrieval gain measured so far, and it costs nothing at inference. Full recall of the annotated span rises from 0.306 to 0.462 and total losses fall from 0.504 to 0.316. The sweep is monotone to 3 and flat beyond (0.403, 0.446, 0.462, 0.463, 0.452, 0.457, 0.457 at 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 8, 12), so 3 is the knee and the adopted default. Every length bucket improves and the long ones most: 2048 tokens 0.356 to 0.493, 4096 0.353 to 0.584, 8192 0.327 to 0.523, 16384 0.366 to 0.581. Every evidence position improves too. The attribution is clean and it settles the ranker question. Applying the same contiguity to the learned R4 ranker gives 0.444 against the heuristic's 0.446 at the same width, so the contiguity is the entire gain and the learned ranking adds nothing on top of it. R3 and R4 stay rejected and no retrieval.json is shipped. The mechanism is that the metric, and a reader, both need an unbroken sentence: the recall score is the longest contiguous run of gold tokens, and the span is a median 38 words spread over several segments. This changes retrieval only, so the symbolic champion C0 is unaffected; the accuracy benefit arrives when a model is trained against the improved evidence.

hypothesis: H1: a compact pretrained cross-encoder scoring (question, candidate, retrieved evidence) beats the symbolic lexical fusion
architecture: MiniLM-L6 cross-encoder (22.9M params), mean pooling, listwise softmax over candidates, fused with the symbolic path by a weighted logit sum with per-kind temperature and a Noul Platt map
dataset_version: data/neural/bench_train.jsonl + train_v1.jsonl, pre-R2/R8 retrieval (140-word quota budget, no local idf, no question expansion, no contiguity)
reason: Clears the bar, and by far less than the model is worth. Dev score 0.5847 to 0.5936, above the 0.005 margin, driven entirely by the hard tier (0.501 to 0.554); standard is flat at 0.534 and easy REGRESSES from 0.679 to 0.660. The gap that matters is elsewhere: the same checkpoint scores 0.715 on the dev subset as a bare cross-encoder and only 0.560 through the engine. The fusion is discarding most of the model. Its weights were fitted to minimise calibration NLL and came out at 0.25 neural against 0.1 symbolic, a 2.5 to 1 ratio that the symbolic logits can outvote wherever their magnitude is larger, so the blend is well calibrated and less accurate than either the neural path alone or a sensible compromise. Promoted because it is a genuine improvement and because it makes the JevBench milestone possible, not because the number is satisfying. Long context is weak as expected: 0.346 overall and 0.296 above 8k tokens, on a model trained against the retrieval that R2 and R8 have since replaced.

hypothesis: The engine was publishing the complement of P(true) for Noul; orienting both fusion terms the same way recovers what the scorer already knew
architecture: E1's MiniLM-L6 cross-encoder unchanged; only the engine's Noul fusion orientation and the fusion fit were corrected, plus the noul_true_index the artifact now declares
reason: The same weights, read the right way round. Dev score 0.5936 to 0.7048 and overall accuracy 0.560 to 0.679, with no retraining and no change to the model. Noul carries it, 0.468 to 0.765 over 1220 of 3037 questions, because the engine had been publishing the exact complement of the probability it intended. Every tier moves: easy 0.660 to 0.785, standard 0.534 to 0.634, hard 0.554 to 0.712. Calibration improves too, ECE 0.088 to 0.058, since the map was no longer fighting an inverted logit. Long context rises 0.346 to 0.405. Against the symbolic champion C0 the margin is now 0.5847 to 0.7048, a gain of 0.120, with easy +0.106, standard +0.099 and hard +0.211. Latency p50 59 ms, peak memory 312 MB, schema validity 1.000, zero errors. The remaining weakness is Score at 0.507 and the judge tier at 0.426, neither of which the orientation touched.
